So if you're thinking about buying a bicycle and you've been shopping around, you may have asked yourself at one point why you should spend 500-1000 dollars on a bike when you can get one at a department store for maybe 100-300.

I'll tell you something you may already have realized. Those department store bikes are pieces of shit. But how shitty are they, exactly? The sad truth is that most people cannot tell the difference!

Where should I start? How about weight? In my opinion, an entry level bike should weigh no more than 25 pounds. The bikes you get from department stores are mostly going to weigh between 30-40 pounds or more. Why is weight so important? Physics. The more weight you're trying to move, the more energy it takes to move it. This might not matter so much if you're riding on flat ground, but it makes a hell of a difference if you have to go up an incline. Suddenly every little bit of weight counts. This is one of the main reasons why pro cyclists are so skinny and their bikes weigh so little. They have to weigh as little as possible or they won't stand a chance in a race.

"But I'm not a pro cyclist, and besides, all that weight will make me go faster down the other side of hills!". You're right. You're not going to need to shave every last gram off the weight of your bike. That would be pointless for you and the vast majority of people. But weight still matters, because you will wear yourself out much faster on a heavy bike, especially if you're not used to riding. Too much weight is also very dangerous on a bicycle when going downhill. It makes turning more difficult and it makes braking distances longer. Someone on a lighter bike has much more maneuverability than you do, which often translates to them being able to outpace you on a downhill stretch if they know what they're doing. Of course, aerodynamics and rolling resistance (tire footprint) also play a part.

In short, weight is an important consideration for cycling, and as a general rule, cheap bikes weigh more. More weight wears you out faster, and is less safe.

Now onto components. Bicycles have bearings and bearing surfaces. Cheap ones are made of cheap material which wears out faster. Bad bearings means the bike moves less efficiently. The most important parts with bearings are the front and rear wheel axles (called hubs) and the axle for the pedal arms (it's called the bottom bracket). For these, sealed bearings are better because they require less maintenance and keep grit away from the bearings. Department store bikes don't come with sealed bearings. They come with the old style cup and cone bearings that require frequent inspection and adjustment. These are far more prone to collect bits of grit from the road. Grit destroys bearings and bearing surfaces. Department store bikes also usually don't have much grease packed in with the bearings either, which means you're basically grinding metal on metal. This leads to lower pedaling efficiency and, once again, faster wear. All of this also means the bike will be prone to making squeaking noises.

In the long run, all this means you'll have to spend more money getting these bearings serviced or replaced. Replacement can sometimes mean having to buy a whole new set of wheels, depending on how badly the hubs are worn.

Now onto the drivetrain. The drivetrain is a collection of components that translate your pedaling force to the rear wheel. Most notably, it consists of the rear cogs, the chain, the front chainrings, the pedal arms, and the pedals. It is the soul of your bike. Skimping on quality here means quicker wear, which means you'll have to replace all this stuff, and it's probably going to end up costing you a considerable chunk of what you spent on the bike to buy it in the first place.

Even the cheapest parts you get at a bike shop will be of better quality than the stuff you'll find on a low end department store bike. I know this from personal experience. I bought a cheap walmart road bike for around 120 dollars and ended up spending 75 bucks on parts to replace the entire drivetrain after the first thousand miles. Since I did the replacements myself, I saved a bit of money, and I also bought the cheapest parts I could get, but I also had to buy a couple tools, which drove up the cost.

There's also simple fact to remember: chains and chainrings/cogs wear out together. A worn chain will cause accelerated wear on the cogs and chainring, and a worn chainring or cogs will cause accelerated wear on the chain. If you ride with low quality materials on the drivetrain, you are going to wear the whole thing out before long.

On to rims. Rims are important. A cheap rim will go out of alignment quickly, or in the worst case scenario, bend and buckle while you're riding, resulting in a potentially dangerous crash and injuries. Department store bikes can come with terrible rim braking surfaces that wear out even before your brake pads have worn! This happened to me. I also had a set of department store bike rims that didn't even have a suitable braking surface. It was nothing but smooth paint where the brakes made contact with the rim. This led to incredibly poor braking performance, which in turn caused repetitive strain injury in my hands form squeezing the brake levers too hard, and also led to one of the cheap brake levers breaking. In the end, I had to replace the brake levers and the rims. Department store bike rims are garbage!

So, this is getting really long. I hope I was able to impress upon you a good understanding of why department store bikes are so bad. Sure they'll work, but they'll end up costing you in the long run, whether that's in parts and repairs or whether that's in your own personal well-being.

All that said, it may not be a bad idea to buy one. Wait, what? Yeah, that's right. If you just want to get your foot in the door and try cycling, and you know what you're getting into with these cheap bikes, then I say go ahead and buy one with the understanding that you're just getting a disposable bike to learn on. It's something that you'll ride until it falls apart, at which point you can chuck it for recycling and buy a REAL bike.
